summary: Surveys a range of authentication technologies and gives protocol designers suggestions about which kinds fit which protocols and applications on the Internet. It is informational guidance, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo surveys ways for network systems to check who sent information. It explains why passwords can fail and why stronger methods depend on secure key management.

questions: how to choose authentication for a protocol
subtitle: A survey of authentication methods and the attacks they are designed to resist.

tldr.problem: Authentication needs differ across systems, but passwords sent over a network can be captured and replayed.
tldr.mechanism: The memo compares authentication by the attacks it resists, explains symmetric and asymmetric cryptography, and discusses user, host, service, and key-management needs.
tldr.outcome: The 1994 memo recommends stronger cryptographic authentication and phasing out mechanisms vulnerable to passive attacks when practical.

today: RFC 1704 is an Informational memo published in October 1994, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. Its recommendations describe the authors' view of authentication needs at that time.

sections.title: Authentication and Network Attacks
sections.content:
Authentication verifies the identity of the source of information. Authorization grants access rights based on an authenticated identity. The memo says authentication needs depend on how a system is used, who can reach it, and how it connects to a network.

A passive attack watches traffic and may record information for later use. An active attack inserts or changes packets. A replay attack resends previously valid messages; constant information such as a password can be reused this way.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication checks who sent information; authorization decides what that identity may access. A password sent unchanged can be captured and reused by an attacker.

sections.title: Authentication by Attack Resistance
sections.content:
The memo describes a range from no authentication to methods designed to resist active attacks. Simple passwords and other constant credentials can be disclosed to an observer and replayed. Non-disclosing methods, such as one-time passwords or challenge-response, address passive capture but can still have other weaknesses.

Stronger systems use the computing abilities of both parties and may authenticate in both directions. They can also establish a shared session key for later exchanges. The memo says the categories are not a strict ranking because different mechanisms fit different problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Some methods reveal the same secret each time, while others use changing challenges or cryptography. Designers must choose a method that addresses the attacks their system faces.

sections.title: Symmetric Keys, Public Keys, and Signatures
sections.content:
Symmetric cryptography uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt information. The parties must receive that key securely. The memo describes Kerberos as a system using a trusted key server that knows users' and services' secret keys.

Asymmetric cryptography uses mathematically related keys for encryption and decryption, which can simplify key distribution. A cryptographic checksum based on a shared secret can provide integrity and authenticate the source, but not non-repudiation. A digital signature can use a public key to verify who signed data and can support non-repudiation.
sections.plainLanguage: A symmetric system requires both parties to protect the same secret key. Public-key systems use related keys, and digital signatures let others check who signed information.

sections.title: Authenticating Users to Remote Hosts
sections.content:
The memo says that plain-text passwords sent by services such as Telnet or rlogin do not protect against replay after an eavesdropper captures them. It recommends at least a non-disclosing password system as a defense against passive attacks.

Perimeter defenses can require a user to authenticate to an externally accessible gateway before reaching internal hosts. The memo calls this a short-term approach because the gateway is not transparent to IP, computer-to-computer authentication is difficult, and a breached perimeter can expose weak internal systems.
sections.plainLanguage: A password sent in plain text can be read and reused by someone watching the network. A non-disclosing method prevents that direct exposure, while a gateway defense has limitations.

sections.title: Key Management and Recommendations
sections.content:
The memo calls key management one of the hardest parts of authentication at internetwork scale. Symmetric systems need secure key distribution; public-key systems can use certificates signed by trusted authorities. The memo notes that published key-management protocols have had subtle flaws.

Its 1994 recommendations are to use strong cryptographic authentication where needed, use public-key technology when practical and cost-effective, and phase out mechanisms vulnerable to passive attack. It also calls for more research on key management and scalable multicast security.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication depends on getting keys to the right parties and keeping them safe. The authors recommend stronger methods and more research into key management.
